what: Remitly runs a digital money-transfer service that lets immigrants send money home from their phones. Customers fund transfers from bank accounts, debit cards or cards and recipients collect cash, receive bank deposits or get mobile-wallet credits in about 170 countries. It earns a fee on each transfer and a spread on the currency exchange.
customers: Immigrants in the United States, Canada, the United Kingdom, Europe and Australia sending money to family in countries such as Mexico, India, the Philippines, Guatemala and Colombia, plus a growing number of small business and higher-value customers.
money: Transaction fees and foreign-exchange spreads on cross-border transfers.
Remitly One membership, business transfers and higher-value sends.
moat: Remittances are a trust business: customers need the money to arrive quickly and safely, and once they have found a service that works they rarely switch. Remitly has built licences in many countries, payout networks with banks and cash agents, and a brand known among migrant communities. Its digital-only model is far cheaper to run than Western Union’s agent stores, which lets it undercut on price.
risks: Changes to US immigration policy could reduce the number of senders or make customers more cautious.
A US excise tax on remittances began in 2026; it targets cash-funded transfers, but further measures could follow.
Competition from Wise, banks, fintech apps and stablecoin-based transfers keeps pressure on fees.
Stock-based compensation is large, so reported free cash flow overstates what owners keep.
Fraud losses and regulatory compliance are constant costs in money transfer.
opportunities: Revenue more than quadrupled from $459M in 2021 to $1.9B over the last twelve months, and the company turned profitable in 2025.
Free cash flow of $395M is about 8.5% of the market value.
The shares trade at about 13 times trailing and forward earnings, with $669M of cash and almost no debt.
Digital share of the roughly $700B remittance market is still rising as customers leave agent locations.
watch: Active customer and send-volume growth, take rate per transfer, the effect of US immigration policy and the remittance tax, and stock-based compensation.
view: Remitly has done what most fintechs promised and few delivered: it grew revenue fourfold since 2021 and then became profitable. It is taking share from Western Union and MoneyGram because sending money from a phone at a lower fee is simply better for the customer, and migrants who find a reliable service tend to stay for years. The business now produces real free cash flow, $395M over the last twelve months.

Two caveats on the headline numbers. First, trailing net income of $364M jumped far faster than operating cash flow, which suggests non-recurring items, most likely tax-related; I would not capitalise it. Second, stock-based compensation is large, so the true owner earnings are lower than the free cash flow line. Even adjusting for both, a valuation of about 13 times earnings and roughly 12 times free cash flow is low for a company still growing revenue at more than 20%.

The reason it is cheap is politics. The market fears that US immigration enforcement and remittance taxes will shrink the customer base, and that is a real risk because the US is the largest sending country. But Remitly’s volume has kept growing through it, the excise tax mainly hits cash-funded transfers rather than its bank and card customers, and it is expanding in Europe and other corridors. I think the discount is larger than the risk, and the stock is attractive for patient investors.
bull: Digital share of remittances keeps rising, Remitly grows above 20% with expanding margins and the political discount fades.
bear: Tougher US immigration policy and new taxes shrink sending volumes just as competition squeezes fees.
